dodClarity.reminder: Run a clarity check to sharpen your DoD.
dodClarity.reminderAmber: Some dimensions of your DoD were flagged. Consider revisiting.
dodClarity.observabilityQuestion: What will be different or exist when this is done — whether that's something you can point to, a skill you've gained, or a change in how things work?
dodClarity.observabilityDescription: When you finish, you should be able to describe what's changed or what exists — whether it's a deliverable, a learned skill, or a concrete outcome. This helps you know when you're actually done.
dodClarity.observabilityTip1: Describe the end state in concrete terms — what someone would see, hear, or measure
dodClarity.observabilityTip2: Avoid abstract words like "better," "more," or "ready" — replace with specifics
dodClarity.controlQuestion: Does this depend on anyone else saying yes or making a decision?
dodClarity.controlDescription: If your goal depends on someone else's decision or approval, you're not fully in control of completion. Either reframe it to focus on what you can do, or be explicit that it depends on them and plan for that uncertainty.
dodClarity.controlTip1: Reframe the goal to focus only on what you can directly do
dodClarity.controlTip2: If it truly depends on someone else, make that explicit in your DoD and plan for contingencies
dodClarity.binaryQuestion: Is done a clear yes-or-no, or does it exist on a scale?
dodClarity.binaryDescription: Goals on a scale like "get better" or "improve" are hard to finish because you never quite reach the end. A clear yes-or-no makes it obvious when you're done and lets you move forward with confidence.
dodClarity.binaryTip1: Replace spectrum words with a clear threshold or checkpoint
dodClarity.binaryTip2: Ask yourself: "How will I know for certain it's done?"
dodClarity.ownershipQuestion: Is this something you genuinely want, or are you doing it because someone else expects it?
dodClarity.ownershipDescription: If you're doing this because someone else wants it, you'll struggle to prioritize it or push through when it gets hard. Make sure this is something you actually care about finishing.
dodClarity.ownershipTip1: If it's mandatory, connect it to something you genuinely care about
dodClarity.ownershipTip2: Ask why this matters beyond the obligation — what's the deeper reason?
dodClarity.decomposabilityQuestion: What's your actual first step — the one you could start today?
dodClarity.decomposabilityDescription: If you can't name your first step right now, try breaking the goal down further — a concrete next action will tell you whether you actually know what you're doing.
dodClarity.decomposabilityTip1: Start by naming your very next action, no matter how small
dodClarity.decomposabilityTip2: If you can't name it, break the goal down further until you can

philosophy.title: Platform Philosophy
philosophy.body: This tracker is built around one principle: clarity before execution. Before you schedule a task, you define what success looks like. The system then organises work from strategic goals down to daily actions, and uses daily review ceremonies to keep everything honest. The flow is always top-down: you know why before you decide what and when.

hierarchy.title: The Goal Hierarchy
hierarchy.intro: Everything lives in one chain: Goals → Milestones → Projects → Actions.
hierarchy.goalDesc: A Goal is a strategic objective — something you're working toward over weeks or months, with a written Definition of Done (DoD) describing exactly when you've succeeded.
hierarchy.milestoneDesc: A Milestone is a sequential phase of that goal, each with its own Definition of Achieved (DoA).
hierarchy.projectDesc: A Project is a focused body of work within a milestone, with its own DoD.
hierarchy.actionDesc: An Action is a single task with an estimated duration and a scheduled date.
hierarchy.example: Example: Goal: "Launch MVP" → Milestone: "Beta ready" → Project: "Auth system" → Actions: "Set up JWT", "Write login page".

goalGroups.title: Goal Groups vs Regular Goals
goalGroups.regular: A regular goal has a timeline, a Definition of Done, and contains milestones and projects directly. It represents a concrete outcome you're driving toward.
goalGroups.group: A goal group is a container — it organises related goals under one name but has no timeline or projects of its own. Think of it as a folder for a domain of your life. Goals inside a group are still independent, each with their own milestones and timelines.
goalGroups.example: Example: "2026 Health" is a goal group containing "Run a marathon" and "Lose 10kg" as separate goals, each with its own milestones.

intervals.title: Intervals vs Routines
intervals.intro: Both intervals and routines generate actions automatically — the difference is when they fire.
intervals.intervalDesc: Intervals run on a schedule you define: every 3 days, every Monday, on the 1st of each month. Use them for recurring work that isn't daily.
intervals.routineDesc: Routines run every single day at specific times you set (e.g. 9am, 2pm, 8pm). Use them for daily practices.
intervals.gathering: Both are checked during Action Gathering each morning and produce actions for today and the next two days.
intervals.example: Example: "Weekly team 1:1" is an interval (every Monday). "Morning pages" is a routine (8am daily).

dailyFlow.title: The Daily Flow
dailyFlow.step1Body: The system checks all active intervals and routines and creates actions for today (and 2 days ahead). Runs automatically when you open Today.
dailyFlow.step2Body: You assign start times to any untimed actions, resolve scheduling conflicts, and decide what to skip or postpone. Ends with "Begin day."
dailyFlow.step3Body: You disposition anything you didn't complete: postpone, outsource, or archive it. Ends with a preview of tomorrow.
dailyFlow.skipping: Skipping a day isn't silent — if yesterday's After-day wasn't completed, the system will ask you to handle it before starting today's Pre-day.

priority.title: The Priority System
priority.intro: Every action gets a priority based on two questions: Is this urgent? Is this important?
priority.p: P — Primary: Urgent + Important. Do it now.
priority.s: S — Secondary: Not urgent, but Important. Schedule it properly.
priority.o: O — Outsource: Urgent, but not Important. Delegate it.
priority.b: B — Bucket List: Neither urgent nor important. Park it for someday.
priority.advice: This is the Eisenhower matrix. A healthy week is mostly S — scheduled, important work — not constant P firefighting. Bucket list items stay visible without cluttering your active work.

actionFates.title: Action Fates
actionFates.intro: When an action doesn't get done, After-day asks what happened. The answer is the action's fate — it keeps your system accurate without losing history.
actionFates.postponed: Postponed — Rescheduled to a future date. The work still matters, just later.
actionFates.outsource: Outsource (WOO) — Delegated. Two follow-up actions are created: one to hand it off, one to confirm it got done.
actionFates.backlog: Backlog — Not important enough to reschedule right now (for linked actions). Stays visible, deprioritised.
actionFates.bucketList: Bucket List — Parked for someday (for standalone actions). No date, no pressure.
actionFates.archived: PassedArchived — No longer relevant. Auto-applied to unlinked interval/routine actions.

dayState.title: DayState Lifecycle
dayState.intro: The system tracks each calendar day through four states:
dayState.state1: Not started — No ceremony run yet.
dayState.state2: Gathering complete — Intervals and routines have been converted to actions for today.
dayState.state3: Pre-day complete — All actions have start times; you've begun the day.
dayState.state4: After-day complete — All incomplete actions have been dispositioned.
dayState.closing: Days that are fully complete show as closed. Incomplete days stay open until After-day is run, which is why the system prompts you to close yesterday before opening today.

hints.goalsList: Goals are your strategic objectives — things you're actively working toward over weeks or months, each with a Definition of Done so you know exactly when you've succeeded. Goals contain Milestones, which contain Projects, which contain Actions — every task in the system traces back to a goal. If you have a broad area of life with multiple independent goals (like "Health" or "Career"), create a Goal Group to organise them without forcing them into a single timeline.
hints.dod: The Definition of Done is a written statement of what "finished" looks like for this goal. A good DoD is observable (you can verify it), binary (yes or no, not "getting better"), and something you actually control. Vague DoDs like "improve my fitness" create drift — concrete ones like "run 5km without stopping" create clarity. Use the clarity check (the ✓ button) to test your DoD across five dimensions.
hints.doa: The Definition of Achieved describes what it looks like when this milestone is complete — what will be true, demonstrated, or delivered. Unlike the goal's DoD (the final finish line), milestones are sequential phases: completing one unlocks the next. A good DoA is concrete enough that a third party could confirm it without explanation from you.
hints.lastMilestone: Marking a milestone as "last" designates it as the final phase of the goal — the one that closes everything out when complete. A goal can only have one last milestone. New milestones you add are automatically inserted before the last one, keeping the final phase pinned at the end of the sequence. This is typically your "ship it", "hand off", or "launch" milestone.
hints.priority: Priority is based on two questions: Is this urgent? Is this important? P (Primary) means both — do it now. S (Secondary) means important but not yet urgent — schedule it properly before it becomes a fire. O (Outsource) means urgent but not important — delegate it. B (Bucket List) means neither — park it for someday. A healthy workload is mostly S; if everything feels P, that's the signal to revisit what's actually important.
hints.intervalsList: Intervals generate actions automatically on a schedule you define — every N days, every Monday, on specific dates. They're for recurring work that isn't daily, like a weekly check-in or a monthly review. When the system gathers actions each morning, it checks all active intervals and creates actions for today and the next two days. Set an end date if the interval has a finite run; leave it open for indefinite recurring work.
hints.intervalRecurrence: The recurrence rule controls when this interval fires. "Every 7 days" counts from the start date. "Every Monday" uses a weekly day-of-week pattern. Use custom dates when the schedule is irregular — the 1st and 15th of each month, or a fixed list of deadlines. The system gathers actions 2 days ahead, so your actions appear before the due date rather than on it.
hints.todayLinkedStandalone: Linked actions belong to a project — they're part of tracked, committed work in your goal hierarchy. Standalone actions are one-offs with no project context, added directly to a day. Both appear on Today, but they're handled differently in After-day: linked actions that go undone require a fate decision (they represent committed project work), while standalone actions are optional to review.
hints.preDayOverlap: An overlap means two actions are scheduled at the same time based on their start time and estimated duration. Overlaps aren't blocked — you can keep them if one is background work or can flex. To resolve one, adjust a start time, postpone an action to another day, or outsource it. All remaining overlaps are shown in the final read-only overview before you begin your day.
hints.afterDayFate: Action fate records what happened to work you didn't complete, keeping your system accurate without losing history. Postpone reschedules to a specific date. Outsource creates two follow-up actions — one to hand it off, one to confirm it's done. Not Important moves it to your backlog (for linked actions). Pass archives it as no longer needed (for interval-generated actions).

0.title: Welcome to Tracker
0.body: Tracker is a structured productivity system built around one idea: the work you do each day should connect to something that matters. It ties your long-term goals to your daily actions through a clear hierarchy, daily rituals, and scheduled intervals — so nothing falls through the cracks.

1.title: Three Ways to Capture Work
1.body: Tracker organizes everything into three dimensions. Goals are your long-term ambitions — the things you're working toward over weeks or months. Intervals are recurring commitments — habits, routines, and time-blocked work that repeat on a schedule. Standalone actions are one-off tasks that don't belong to anything larger. All three feed into your day.

2.title: How Goals Break Down
2.body: Goals decompose into smaller, ordered units. A goal is complete when all its milestones are closed. A milestone closes when you mark it done. Projects hold the day-to-day actions that get gathered into your schedule. You always know where each action fits.

3.title: Recurring Work
3.body: Intervals are repeating commitments with a recurrence schedule — daily standups, weekly reviews, monthly check-ins. Routines are simpler: they repeat every day. At gathering time, Tracker creates actions from your active intervals and routines and places them in the right days automatically. You set the schedule once; Tracker handles the rest.

4.title: Three Daily Rituals
4.step1Body: Before you start, assign start times to your actions and resolve any overlaps. This ritual gates the Today view.
4.step2Body: Your working view. Linked actions from goals and intervals sit at the top; standalone tasks below. Add quick tasks inline as the day unfolds.
4.step3Body: Close the day by deciding the fate of each unfinished action: postpone it, send it to backlog, outsource it, or mark it done. Closing triggers gathering for the next two days.

5.title: Who Can Share Journals With You?
5.body: Journals can be shared with other users by email. For someone to add you to their journal, they need to look you up by email first — but only if you allow it. Make your choice below. You can change this any time in Settings.
5.stateOn: Others can find me by email
5.hint: You can change this later in Settings.

6.title: Let's Get Started
6.body: That's all you need to know for now. The best place to begin is creating your first goal — the Goal Wizard will walk you through it step by step. Under Tools you'll also find the Skills labs: six short practice sessions for working with AI, which you can pick up any time. Or if you want a deeper reference on any concept, the Guide page has it all.
6.ctaToday: Finish — I’ll explore on my own

today.step1Body: Today shows every action scheduled for today — whether it came from a goal, an interval, or was added manually. Before you can see it fully, the Pre-day ritual must be completed to assign start times and resolve any conflicts.
today.step2Body: Actions that come from goals or intervals appear in the Linked section — they're part of something larger. Actions you add directly from this page appear in Standalone. The split keeps structured work and quick tasks visually separate.
today.step3Body: Type in the input at the top of Standalone to add a task on the fly. Once you start typing, fields for date, estimated time, and start time appear. Hit Enter or the plus button to add it. That's it.

pre-day.step1Body: Pre-day is the planning gate that runs before your Today view opens. You review the actions gathered for today, assign start times to each one, and make sure your schedule holds together. Skipping it means Today remains locked.
pre-day.step2Body: Each action needs a start time before the day can begin. Untimed actions — those without an assigned time — block the ritual from completing. Work through them in order, or defer any you're not ready to schedule.
pre-day.step3Body: If two actions are scheduled at the same time, Tracker flags the conflict. You'll see a warning on the overlapping action. Resolve it by adjusting the start time or estimated duration before proceeding.

after-day.step1Body: After-day is the reflection ritual. At the end of each day, you review every action that wasn't marked done and decide what happens to it. This is how Tracker stays clean — nothing carries forward silently.
after-day.step2Body: For each unfinished action you choose a fate: Done — it was completed after all. Postpone — reschedule it to a future date. Backlog — return it to the project backlog without a date. Outsource — it's someone else's now. Bucket list — a someday idea, not urgent. Archive — it's no longer relevant.
after-day.step3Body: Once you close the day, Tracker runs gathering for the next two days — pulling in actions from your active intervals and routines. Your tomorrow is already partially populated before you sleep.

goals-list.step1Body: A goal is the highest level of intent in Tracker — something you're working toward that takes sustained effort. Beneath each goal sits an ordered sequence of milestones, and beneath each milestone, projects and actions. The progress bar on each goal reflects how far through the milestone sequence you are.
goals-list.step2Body: Goals can be standalone or grouped. A goal group is a container that holds related goals together — useful when a large ambition breaks into several independent parallel tracks. Regular goals stand alone. Both types behave the same way internally; the group is just an organizational wrapper.

manage-goal.step1Body: The milestones on this page are ordered checkpoints on the way to your goal. They run sequentially — completing one unlocks the focus on the next. Each milestone has a definition of achievement that makes it clear what done means for that checkpoint.
manage-goal.step2Body: The progress bar at the top reflects milestone completion: how many milestones are closed out of the total. It doesn't measure effort or time — only closed milestones count. The current milestone is the first unclosed one in the sequence.
manage-goal.step3Body: Inside each milestone, projects hold the day-to-day work. The Story view lets you see all milestones and their projects together on one scrollable page — useful for getting a sense of the whole arc of a goal at once.

projects-list.step1Body: A project is a body of work that lives inside a milestone. It holds a set of actions and has a definition of done that describes what completion looks like. A project's status — Active, Complete, or Blocked — is computed from the state of its actions and whether the definition of done condition is met.
projects-list.step2Body: Every project belongs to a milestone, which belongs to a goal. You can view all projects across all goals here, or navigate to a specific goal to see just its projects in context. Projects without a milestone aren't possible — the hierarchy is always intact.

intervals-list.step1Body: Intervals are recurring commitments on a schedule — they can repeat daily, weekly, monthly, or on custom patterns. Routines are a simpler variant that repeat every day without configuration. Both generate actions automatically.
intervals-list.step2Body: Each interval has a recurrence rule — which days of the week, which weeks of the month, or a custom pattern. At gathering time, Tracker evaluates which intervals are due and creates actions for those days. You set the rule once; Tracker creates the work.
intervals-list.step3Body: Actions generated from intervals appear in the Linked section of Today automatically. You don't need to do anything — gathering runs in the background when you open Today, and again after After-day completes. If an interval is paused or inactive, its actions won't be generated.

calendar.step1Body: The calendar shows scheduled actions — those with an assigned date and start time. Actions without a start time don't appear here. Milestones with target dates are also shown as markers. It's a time-view into your workload, not a complete task list.
calendar.step2Body: Use the filter controls to narrow what's shown — by goal, by interval, or by action type. This is useful when you want to see how a single goal's work is distributed across time, or when the calendar feels too dense and you want to focus on one track.

journals.step1Body: Journals are running records — narrative logs of thought, progress, and experience, optionally anchored to a goal or project. Unlike structured task lists, journals tell the story of the work. Entries are chronological and permanent: you can archive them but not delete them.
journals.step2Body: Journals can be shared with other users. Everyone on the access list can add entries — there's no elevated permission tier. To add someone, you look them up by email. They'll only be found if they've opted into discoverability in their settings.
journals.step3Body: A quick-add input at the bottom of your Today view lets you drop a thought into any journal without navigating away. It defaults to your default journal but you can redirect it to any active journal on the fly.

hub.subtitle: Six short labs, each training one habit that decides whether working with AI helps or hurts — saying precisely what you want, breaking a problem down, checking what comes back, and knowing when to rely on it. Each one stands on its own, and they can be done in any order.

how.title: What a sitting is
how.premise: Every lab runs the same shape, and it is short. One sitting is a few minutes, not an evening.

intro.step1Title: A place to practise one thing
intro.step1Body: Evidence Lab is a training tool. It trains a single skill: deciding whether to believe what an AI has just told you. It's self-contained — nothing you do here touches your goals, projects or calendar unless you ask it to.
intro.step2Title: Confident and wrong look the same
intro.step2Body: AI answers are fluent whether or not they're accurate. No wording, formatting or tone reliably separates the two, so the only thing that works is stepping outside the answer and checking. That's a habit, and habits need repetitions.
intro.step3Title: One item at a time, about a minute each
intro.step3Body: You'll see a question someone asked and the answer an AI gave. You check it however you like — searches open in a new tab — then commit a verdict before anything is revealed, and then you find out. Most people do five or six in a sitting.
intro.step4Title: You commit before you see the answer
intro.step4Body: Your verdict and your confidence are locked in first. It's deliberate and slightly uncomfortable: it's the only way to learn what you would actually have concluded, rather than what you'd have said afterwards.
intro.step5Title: Roughly a third of the answers are correct
intro.step5Body: Flagging a true answer costs you exactly what missing a false one costs. The skill is telling them apart, not being vigilant — someone who suspects everything scores badly here, and the scoring is built to make that visible.
intro.step6Title: Six short modules, then open practice
intro.step6Body: Each module teaches one move — noticing when a claim is worth checking, reading a citation as a claim, going to an independent source — and has items to practise it. Progress is tracked per module and reviews return on a widening schedule. No streaks: nothing breaks if you skip a week.

how.title: How a drill works
how.premise: Every item is one realistic exchange: somebody asked a question, an AI answered. Some answers are accurate. Some contain a fault — an invented source, a figure that expired, a real study cited for something it doesn't say. Nothing in the writing tells you which kind you're looking at.
how.readTitle: Read the question, then the answer
how.readBody: They're shown in two separate boxes. The top one is what was asked; the one below it is what the AI replied. Only the reply is being judged.
how.checkBody: Use "Check another source", run a search — it opens in a new tab — and paste back the link and the line that settles it. Forty seconds is the target, not five minutes.
how.commitBody: Choose a verdict, say which part fails if any does, and set how confident you are. This locks the item.
how.revealBody: You see the correct verdict, an explanation of what a fast correct check would have looked like, and how your attempt scored.
how.catchTitle: The one thing worth knowing before you start
how.catchBody: Checking means finding out, not finding fault. Flagging a correct answer counts against you exactly as much as missing a faulty one — and the headline score, telling true from false, is precisely the gap between the two.
how.privacy: Searches open in your own browser tab: Evidence Lab records that you searched and when, never what you searched or what you read. No AI service is involved anywhere — every item is scored against an answer key written in advance.

intro.step1Title: A place to practise one thing
intro.step1Body: Clarity Lab trains a single skill: saying precisely what you want, with enough context for someone to act on it. It's self-contained — nothing here touches your goals, projects or calendar unless you ask it to.
intro.step2Body: Specific prompt tricks expire as models change. What doesn't expire is the thing underneath them — being clear about what you want, for whom, and how you'll know it worked. That's ordinary good writing, and it was useful long before there was anything to prompt.
intro.step3Title: Your text was clear to you
intro.step3Body: That's the whole problem. Once you know what you meant, you can't really read your own sentence as a stranger would. So the tool doesn't tell you your writing was unclear — it shows you what a reader actually did with it, and lets the gap do the teaching.
intro.step4Title: A sitting is longer than a drill
intro.step4Body: 8 to 15 minutes, about once a week. You'll produce one piece of writing and at least one revision of it. If this ever starts to feel like a daily drill, something has gone wrong — clarity is trained by revising, not by repetition.
intro.step5Body: Six criteria, on screen the whole time, including while you write. Writing toward them is the intended behaviour. They're each a checkable feature — "does the request appear in the first two sentences?" — rather than a judgement about whether something felt clear.
intro.step6Title: You commit before you see the score
intro.step6Body: On most items you'll first say which criteria you think failed. Only then are the levels shown. Naming why something didn't work is the half of this skill that carries to the next thing you write, so it gets measured separately.

how.title: How a sitting works
how.premise: Each item gives you something to write or something to fix. Some are drills of a single sentence; most are a short piece of writing and a rewrite of it. Everything is scored against the same six criteria you can see on the right.
how.readBody: Some items include a context sheet — facts only you know. Deciding which of them the reader actually needs is part of the exercise, not a formality.
how.writeBody: A plain box: no autocomplete, no suggestions, no assistant. The tool is training your composition, and a helper in the box would train the helper.
how.diagnoseBody: Before any score appears, you tag the criteria you think went wrong. Your tags versus what actually failed is its own result.
how.scoreBody: One per criterion, each with the line from your own text that justified it. The total comes last, because it's the least useful thing on the screen.
how.reviseBody: The draft stays visible and locked. The difference between the two is the number worth watching — and it should shrink over time, as the skill moves into your first draft.
how.lockBody: A diagnosis entered after you've seen the scores isn't a diagnosis, it's a recollection. Same for predicting what a reader will do. Both get committed first and can't be edited afterwards — that's the only way to find out what you'd actually have concluded.

decomposition.title: Decomposition Lab
decomposition.subtitle: Training one thing: breaking a messy problem into pieces you can actually check. Not a prompting technique — the habit of decomposing so you know what you're asking for, which doesn't expire when the model does.

how.title: How a sitting works
how.premise: Every item is one messy problem — a move, a party, a renovation — and your job is to turn it into pieces somebody could actually check off. Nothing here is graded on how clever the pieces are; it is graded on whether the structure holds together.
how.stateBody: In your own words, say what the undivided problem is and how you would know it was finished. This happens before any piece exists, and the order is recorded.
how.breadthTitle: Name every top-level piece before opening any of them.
how.breadthBody: All the main parts first, even roughly. Then go back and break each one down.
how.boundTitle: Give each piece a done condition.
how.boundBody: Something with a date, a count, or a state change in it — a thing someone else could check without asking you.
how.dependBody: Two pieces are dependent when one genuinely cannot start until the other finishes. Writing them in an order does not make that order real.
how.revealBody: You see how the structure scored, which required pieces were missing, and which pairs overlapped.
how.catchTitle: The one thing worth knowing before you start
how.catchBody: Some items are meant to be left alone. If a task is already one checkable action, splitting it is a fault, not thoroughness — the same fault as leaving a huge task whole, seen from the other side.

decomposition.sittingLength: Most items take two to ten minutes: state the whole, build the breakdown, see what it missed.

intro.step2Title: This is not a prompting trick
intro.step2Body: Breaking a task into steps and handing them to a model one at a time is a real technique, and it's fading — newer models already do that internally. What survives every model change is decomposing so *you* know what you're asking for. That's the whole tool.

intro.step6Title: About a third of items are a trick question
intro.step6Body: Some tasks are already one checkable piece. Splitting them anyway isn't rigor — it's a different failure with the same shape as missing a piece, and it's scored that way.

verification.title: Verification Lab
verification.subtitle: Training one thing: deciding whether an answer is actually right — naming an oracle before you look, designing a check that could fail, and running it. Not a checklist. A checklist that returns the same result either way has already failed you.

how.title: How a sitting works
how.premise: Every item is one artifact with a claim in it — an invoice, a quote, a calculation. Some are correct. Some contain exactly one fault. Nothing in how it is written tells you which.
how.oracleBody: An oracle is just the thing that would settle it: the source, document or recomputation that would tell you whether this is right. You name it before you can see what checks are available, so it is your idea rather than a pick from a menu.
how.benchTitle: Pick your checks from the bench.
how.benchBody: Each check costs time. Some bear on the claim, some do not, and some cannot come back wrong at all — those last ones feel like diligence and prove nothing.
how.verdictBody: Supported, unsupported, or cannot verify — plus which element failed if one did, and what you would still be exposed to if you were wrong.
how.revealBody: You see whether your checks could have caught the fault, whether your verdict matched, and what the cheapest sufficient check would have been.
how.catchTitle: The one thing worth knowing before you start
how.catchBody: A check that could not have come back wrong is not a check. Asking the artifact to grade itself, or re-reading it more carefully, will never fail — so it cannot tell you anything, however thorough it feels.

verification.modulesSubtitle: Six, each training one criterion of the rubric. You don't have to do them in order.
verification.rubricHint: Kept on screen the whole time, including during the reveal. It's the thing being taught, not a hidden grading scheme.

intro.step1Title: A place to practise one thing
intro.step1Body: Verification Lab trains deciding whether an AI answer is actually right. It's self-contained — nothing here touches your goals, projects or calendar unless you ask it to.
intro.step2Title: You name the oracle before you look
intro.step2Body: Before any check runs, you write down what would actually tell you whether the answer is right. That order is locked in and measured — a check chosen after the fact isn't the same move.
intro.step3Title: Cost is always visible, outcomes never are — until you spend
intro.step3Body: Every check on the bench shows what it costs before you run it. Running one is irreversible. That's the entire decision this tool is built around.
intro.step4Title: Two costumes are on the bench on purpose
intro.step4Body: "Ask the model if it's sure" and "ask for a confidence score" are the two things most widely taught as verification, and both return the same thing whether or not the answer is wrong. They're always there, priced cheap, so you can learn to recognise them rather than just be told about them.
intro.step5Title: A correct answer reached by ritual is scored as ritual, not as success
intro.step5Body: If every check you ran could have returned the same result either way, the reveal says so before it says whether you were right. A right answer with no real check behind it is the failure this tool exists to catch.
intro.step6Body: About a third of items have nothing on the bench that can settle them. Recognising that and saying so is scored correct — inventing a check that only feels like it settles things is worse than admitting there isn't one.

delegation.title: Delegation Lab
delegation.subtitle: Training calibrated delegation: knowing when the AI's judgement should lead and when yours should. You estimate first, see advice, and revise — how far you move is the measurement, not a score you're chasing.

how.title: How a sitting works
how.premise: Most items ask you to estimate something you cannot look up, then show you what an advisor said, then let you change your answer. What is measured is how far you moved — not whether you were right.
how.estimateBody: A number, and how confident you are in it. The advice does not exist until this is locked, which is what makes the movement mean anything.
how.adviceBody: Sometimes there is a cue about whether this advisor is good at this particular thing. A cue about the whole category — “AI is good at maths” — is not that.
how.reviseBody: Keep your number, take theirs, or land somewhere between. All three are legitimate; the question is whether the distance you moved matched what the advice was worth.
how.revealBody: You see the truth, where all three answers sat, how far you moved, and whether moving helped you or cost you.
how.catchTitle: The one thing worth knowing before you start
how.catchBody: Not moving is a decision too, and it is scored like one. Sticking with your own answer when the advice was better costs exactly as much as following advice that was worse.

delegation.nullNote: Self-assessment calibration and reliance discrimination are shown as two separate lines on purpose, with no arrow drawn between them. The first reliably improves with practice. Whether it changes how you weigh advice is an open question in the research — and this screen shows you the part that moved and the part that didn't, rather than folding both into one number that would always look like progress.

intro.step1Title: A place to practise one thing
intro.step1Body: Delegation Lab trains knowing when to trust AI advice and when to trust your own judgement. It's self-contained — nothing here touches your goals, projects or calendar unless you ask it to.
intro.step2Title: You estimate before you see any advice
intro.step2Body: Your guess and your confidence are locked in first. The advice doesn't exist on screen until then — otherwise your revision would just be hindsight.
intro.step3Body: Over-reliance and under-reliance are shown side by side, always. A single "reliance" figure would hide the exact trade the research warns about — fixing one failure by making the other worse.
intro.step4Body: Weight of advice is never shown while you're deciding — only afterward. Seeing it live would turn the decision into an exercise in hitting a number instead of actually weighing the advice.
intro.step5Title: The capability list, dated and struck through
intro.step5Body: "AI is good at X, bad at Y" is a snapshot of one model generation. One module shows a list like that from eighteen months ago and which claims already expired — naming the costume works better than warning against it.
intro.step6Title: This tool might not work — and says so
intro.step6Body: Published research on training this skill mostly comes back negative. If your self-assessment improves here while your actual reliance on advice doesn't move, that's not a failed exercise — it's what the research predicts, and it's shown to you plainly rather than hidden.

monitoring.title: Monitoring Lab
monitoring.subtitle: Training self-monitoring: noticing your own state while something is actively shaping it. Every item collects a claim you make about yourself, then measures it against what actually happened.

how.title: How a sitting works
how.premise: Every item collects a claim you make about your own state — will I get this right, do I understand this, did that change my mind — and then puts it next to what actually happened.
how.predictBody: Whether you will get it right, or how well you understand it. The answer field does not exist until this is locked — not hidden, absent.
how.doBody: Answer the question, write the explanation, or read the conversation, depending on the item.
how.compareTitle: See it next to what happened.
how.compareBody: Your claim and the outcome, side by side. That pair is the measurement.
how.windowBody: Two of the six criteria are measured across a window of sittings rather than one at a time, so a single item shows you the outcome and adds a data point — the lab page reports the score once there are enough.
how.catchTitle: The one thing worth knowing before you start
how.catchBody: Guessing high on every prediction does not help. What is measured is whether your confidence separates the ones you get right from the ones you do not — being uniformly confident scores the same as being uniformly unsure.

intro.step1Body: Every item here collects a claim you make about yourself — that you'll get something right, that you understand something, that an agreement didn't sway you — and only then measures it. This is the one tool in the engine that measures a gap about you, not about the world.
intro.step2Title: The prediction locks in before the answer exists
intro.step2Body: You commit first. The answer field doesn't exist on screen until you have — otherwise a prediction made with the answer already visible isn't a prediction.
intro.step3Body: Resolution — can you tell which of your answers are wrong — is confounded with plain performance wherever guessing is possible. So it's always shown next to your performance, never alone.
intro.step4Title: Explaining is the check reading never is
intro.step4Body: Rating how well you understand something, then trying to explain it, reliably drops your own rating — often one or two points on a ten-point scale. Watching that drop happen to your own number is the lesson; nothing here scores the drop itself.
intro.step5Body: Chatbots agree with people far more than another person would, and that agreement carries no information about whether you're right. One module trains noticing that; a different tool (Verification Lab) trains what to do about it.
intro.step6Title: The fix for losing focus can't be "pay more attention"
intro.step6Body: Complacency under repeated, mostly-reliable automation shows up in novices and experts alike, and isn't fixed by trying harder. The module about it scores a structural check — one that fires on its own — higher than a resolution to be more careful.
